paper_title: ThinkDrag: Semantic Drag-Based Image Editing with Visual Reasoning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Drag-based image editing provides an intuitive interface for spatially controlled image manipulation by allowing users to specify handle and target points. Existing methods have made substantial progress through optimization-based, one-step, and feed-forward formulations, but they often interpret drag instructions as geometric displacements. This limits their effectiveness when the desired edit depends on interpreting image content and inferring a plausible semantic transformation from sparse point constraints. We introduce ThinkDrag, a unified multimodal framework for drag-based image editing with visual reasoning. ThinkDrag is trained to associate point constraints with meaningful object- and scene-level transformations, and can optionally produce an explicit reasoning trace that interprets the intended edit before image generation. This reasoning trace improves interpretability, particularly for ambiguous drags. Drag Endpoint Markers, motivated by an analysis of cross-image attention, provide an explicit correspondence signal that grounds each drag in image space. To support this framework, we construct a supervised dataset of semantic drag transformations paired with reasoning traces and introduce DragBench++, a benchmark targeting challenging drag-based editing scenarios with reference edit solutions. Experiments show that ThinkDrag achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving generation quality and plausibility while maintaining competitive point-following precision.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Drag-based image editing provides an intuitive interface for spatially controlled image manipulation by allowing users to specify handle and target points. Existing methods have made substantial progress through optimization-based, one-step, and feed-forward formulations, but they often interpret drag instructions as geometric displacements. This limits their effectiveness when the desired edit depends on interpreting image content and inferring plausible semantic transformation from sparse point constraints. We introduce THINKDRAG, unified multimodal framework for drag-based image editing with visual reasoning. THINKDRAG is trained to associate point constraints with meaningful objectand scene-level transformations, and can optionally produce an explicit reasoning trace that interprets the intended edit before image generation. This reasoning trace improves interpretability, particularly for ambiguous drags. Drag Endpoint Markers, motivated by an analysis of cross-image attention, provide an explicit correspondence signal that grounds each drag in image space. To support this framework, we construct supervised dataset of semantic drag transformations paired with reasoning traces and introduce DragBench++, benchmark targeting challenging drag-based editing scenarios with reference edit solutions. Experiments show that THINKDRAG achieves state-of-theart performance, improving generation quality and plausibility while maintaining competitive point-following precision.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Image editing is fundamental problem in generative modeling, where model must modify visual content while keeping the rest of the scene intact (Meng et al., 2022; Hertz et al., 2023; Brooks et al., 2023). Beyond content creation, it also tests how well model connects visual understanding with controllable synthesis (Deng et al., 2025). Text-guided editing has made image manipulation more accessible, but language alone often provides limited spatial precision. Many edits are easier to specify by directly indicating where visual content should move, such as repositioning an object part or changing pose. Drag-based image editing (Pan et al., 2023; Shi et al., 2024) provides this interface by allowing users to specify pairs of handle and target points, after which the model edits the image by moving the content associated with each handle point toward its target. Early methods such as DragGAN (Pan et al., 2023) demonstrated drag-based editing with GAN priors, while diffusion-based methods extended it to broader visual domains (Shi et al., 2024; Mou et al., 2024). Existing approaches typically rely on latent optimization (Zhang et al., 2025; Xia et al., 2025), one-step latent editing (Zhao et al., 2024; Pu et al., 2026), or feed-forward generation conditioned on point coordinates (Shin et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2025). However, they largely treat drag instructions as spatial displacements and rely on the base generative prior for plausibility. This is limiting because the same handletarget displacement can correspond to different valid edits depending on the object and on what the user intends. For example, moving point on an articulated object may require rotating part rather than translating local patch. Recent unified multimodal models (Zhou et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2025a; Deng et al., 2025) provide new opportunity for drag-based image editing. Unlike conventional image editors designed primarily around synthesis (Brooks et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2025a; Black Forest Labs, 2025), these models couple visual and language understanding with image generation in single framework. This extends the intuition behind DragGAN (Pan et al., 2023): if generative prior enables drag editing within limited domain, then unified multimodal models can provide broader prior for arbitrary images by

sections.content: Figure 1: THINKDRAG handles challenging and ambiguous drags, optionally making its interpretation explicit as reasoning trace that the user can refine, while the drags keep the edit spatially grounded. drawing on their knowledge of the visual world. Such prior is particularly suitable for drag-based editing, where point instruction is not simply displacement vector but an under-specified editing request. Executing it correctly requires understanding what the scene contains and how its objects can move or change. We therefore formulate drag-based editing as semantic interpretation coupled with correspondence-grounded generation. In this work, we introduce THINKDRAG, unified multimodal framework for drag-based image editing with visual reasoning. Given an input image and drag instructions, THINKDRAG generates an edited image that satisfies the point constraints while preserving the semantic structure of the scene. This is enabled by our new dataset of high-quality semantic drag edits, which teach the model to associate sparse point constraints with plausible objectand scene-level transformations, paired with reasoning traces that teach it to interpret the intended edit before generation. To execute drags precisely, we further introduce Drag Endpoint Markers (DEM). Motivated by the observation that each region of the edited image attends predominantly to the source region from which its content originates, DEM explicitly encodes the correspondence between each handle and its target. As illustrated in Figure 1, THINKDRAG uses visual reasoning to interpret ambiguous drag instructions and can further incorporate user text when additional semantic guidance is provided. The model can edit directly, or first reason when the edit is ambiguous or requires higher-level scene understanding. We evaluate THINKDRAG on standard drag-editing benchmarks and introduce DragBench++, new benchmark targeting more challenging scenarios that require higher-level scene understanding and semantic interpretation of point constraints. Extensive experiments show that THINKDRAG achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving generation quality while maintaining competitive pointfollowing precision. The direct editing mode already performs strongly, reflecting the value of semantic drag supervision and unified multimodal modeling. The reasoning mode complements direct editing by making the models interpretation explicit, and it is particularly useful for ambiguous multi-drag edits. In user study, participants prefer THINKDRAG to prior methods in 80% of the overall-preference votes on DragBench++ and 61% on DragBench. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce THINKDRAG, unified multimodal framework for drag-based image editing with visual reasoning, interpreting drag instructions with scene semantics and object structure. We construct, to our knowledge, the first supervised dataset of high-quality semantic drag transformations with reasoning traces for training drag-based image editing models. We propose DragBench++, benchmark targeting more challenging and semantically ambiguous drag-based editing scenarios, with reference edit solutions. We achieve state-of-the-art results on drag-based editing benchmarks and support joint text-drag conditioning, where text disambiguates user intent and drags provide precise spatial control.

sections.title: 2.1 UNIFIED MULTIMODAL UNDERSTANDING AND GENERATION
sections.content: Multimodal understanding and image generation have traditionally followed different modeling paradigms, with autoregressive vision-language models driving perception and reasoning (Liu et al.,

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: 2023a; 2024b; Bai et al., 2023), and diffusion models dominating high-fidelity synthesis (Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021; Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021). Recent unified multimodal models combine both capabilities in single framework, either by tokenizing images and modeling them jointly with text through next-token prediction (Chameleon Team, 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2025) or by coupling autoregressive language modeling with diffusion-based visual generation (Xie et al., 2025b; Zhou et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025; Liao et al., 2025). Multimodal chain-of-thought (Wang et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024) and generator-coupled reasoning (Qin et al., 2026; He et al., 2026) further show growing ability to connect visual perception, language reasoning, and image synthesis, but their use for spatially grounded image manipulation remains underexplored.

sections.title: 2.2 DRAG-BASED IMAGE EDITING
sections.content: Drag-based image editing provides intuitive image manipulation by dragging user-specified handle points to target positions. DragGAN (Pan et al., 2023) introduced this paradigm through latent optimization with motion supervision and point tracking, but its GAN prior limits generalization to arbitrary real images. Diffusion-based methods extend drag editing to broader domains, mostly through test-time optimization (Shi et al., 2024; Mou et al., 2024; Hou et al., 2024; Ling et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024a; Cui et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025; Choi et al., 2025; Xia et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2025) or faster one-step and training-free alternatives (Nie et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2024; Lu & Han, 2025; Yin et al., 2026; Pu et al., 2026; Jhong et al., 2026; He et al., 2025). Most related to our work are feed-forward methods that frame drag-based editing as conditional generation. InstantDrag (Shin et al., 2024) and LightningDrag (Shi et al., 2025) synthesize edited images directly from point or motion conditions derived from videos, treating drags as geometric constraints, while Cui et al. (2024) infer the intended edit with an LLM at test time. In contrast, THINKDRAG interprets drag instructions within unified multimodal model and grounds edits through an explicit correspondence signal in image space, learned from semantic drag edits.

sections.title: 3.1 DATASET CONSTRUCTION
sections.content: Prior work (Shin et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2025) has shown that videos provide natural source of paired supervision for drag-based image editing. These pipelines typically sample source and target images from temporal window and recover motion using optical flow or point tracking. However, video-derived supervision has several limitations. Extracted correspondences are primarily geometric and may not reflect semantically meaningful edit intent, optical flow can be unreliable under large displacement or occlusion, and natural videos often contain camera motion or background variation that corrupts the desired edit supervision. We therefore construct the THINKDRAG dataset, new drag-based image editing dataset that emphasizes high-quality image pairs and semantically meaningful point instructions. Figure 2 gives an overview of the pipeline, described below. Synthetic Image Pair Generation. Drag-based image editing is best suited to transformations that can be expressed through spatial motion of existing visual content, such as object translation, pose change, non-rigid deformation, and local geometric warping. It is less appropriate for edits involving semantic discontinuities (e.g., object insertion and removal, or global style transfer). Based on this distinction, we construct synthetic image pairs through an automated MLLM-assisted pipeline. We first use an MLLM (Bai et al., 2025) to generate diverse source-image prompts from pool of subjects and environments, and synthesize source images using state-of-the-art text-to-image models, including Qwen-Image (Wu et al., 2025a), FLUX.2 (Black Forest Labs, 2026), and Z-Image (Cai et al., 2025). Given each source image, the MLLM proposes image-specific edit prompts constrained to be compatible with drag-like transformations. The source image and edit prompt are then passed to the editing model FLUX.2 (Black Forest Labs, 2026; fal, 2025) to synthesize the target image, and an MLLM-based binary filter discards low-quality or invalid pairs. Semantic Keypoint Matching. From the filtered pairs, we recover each edit as semantic drag instructions. We prompt Gemini 3 Pro (Google, 2025) to identify keypoints that explain the transformation between the source and target images. Each drag consists of handle point, target point, and semantic description of the matched element in both images. This converts the synthetic pair into

Figure 3: Diverse examples of the THINKDRAG dataset. drag-based supervision while preserving the semantic role of each correspondence. Unlike videoderived annotations from optical flow, this procedure targets the user-facing edit intent rather than only low-level motion. Since MLLMs can hallucinate incorrect matches, we validate the predicted correspondences using DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025) features and manual inspection. Reasoning Chain Creation. Finally, we generate reasoning chains for each drag-edit example using Gemini 3 Flash (Google, 2025). The dataset construction pipeline makes the intended edit recoverable by construction: the MLLM has access to the source image, edited image, edit prompt, and semantic keypoint correspondence annotations. We use this information to prompt the MLLM to produce reasoning chain that explains the source scene, interprets each drag in semantic terms, and summarizes the intended transformation while specifying which regions should remain unchanged. Since each sourcetarget pair can be used bidirectionally, we generate reasoning chains for both edit directions. These traces provide supervision for reasoning-driven drag-based editing. Dataset Statistics. Starting from approximately 193K generated pairs, MLLM filtering retains 97K, keypoint matching 50K, and verification yields the final dataset of approximately 11K sourcetarget image pairs from 7K source images. Since each pair can be used in both directions, by swapping the source and target images and reversing the drag endpoints, this yields approximately 22K drag-based editing samples. During training, we further apply standard spatial augmentations such as horizontal flips and random crops. Figure 3 shows how the dataset spans diverse semantic drag transformations. Samples contain 2.15 drags on average (74% with multiple drags) and reasoning traces of 123 words on average. Edit category distribution and per-stage details are provided in Appendix C.

sections.title: 3.2 DRAG CONDITIONING IN A UNIFIED MULTIMODAL MODEL
sections.content: We build on BAGEL (Deng et al., 2025), unified multimodal model with mixture-of-transformers architecture (Liang et al., 2025), and adapt it to drag-based editing by representing drag instructions through its existing multimodal interface. As shown in Figure 4, rather than introducing separate point encoder or treating drags only as low-level geometric inputs, we express each drag through both structured text tokens and spatial endpoint markers. The text tokens expose the paired source and target coordinates, normalized to [0, 1] with three decimals, to the model in form compatible

The endpoint markers complement this representation by injecting the same drag information at the corresponding VAE token locations, providing explicit spatial anchors for image generation through the models generation expert. This design is motivated by the observation that each region of the generated image attends predominantly to the source region from which its content originates (Figure 8). sections.title: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Benchmarks. We evaluate on DragBench (Shi et al., 2024), the standard benchmark for drag-based image editing. We also introduce DragBench++, new benchmark constructed using our dataset construction pipeline in Sec. 3.1 for image pair generation. DragBench++ contains 145 samples with manually annotated drag instructions and emphasizes scenarios that require higher-level scene understanding, object-level reasoning, and semantic interpretation, with more drags per sample and longer displacements than DragBench  (Table 2)  . Unlike prior benchmarks, each input also includes pseudo-ground-truth edited image as reference. Although drag-based editing is under-constrained and multiple outputs may satisfy the same instruction, this reference edit verifies that each example has at least one plausible solution. It also enables reference-based evaluation and more controlled analysis of whether existing metrics reflect meaningful editing quality. Reference edits are used only for evaluation. Baselines that require an edit mask receive manually annotated masks. Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate along two axes: editing accuracy and generation quality. For editing accuracy, we follow prior work (Shi et al., 2024) and report Mean Distance (MD), which measures the distance between each target point and the corresponding handle point tracked in the generated image using DIFT (Tang et al., 2023), restricted to the edit mask. On DragBench++, reference edits show that DIFT-based correspondence can be unreliable under semantic ambiguity or large structural changes. We therefore also report MDMLLM, which uses the same distance definition but replaces DIFT with GPT-5.5 (OpenAI, 2026) for point tracking, computed for the strongest method of each category (Appendix B.2). Since GPT-5.5 is not used in our data pipeline, data construction and evaluation are decoupled. For generation quality, we report Image Fidelity (IF) and FID (Heusel et al., 2017). Following prior work, IF is computed as 1 LPIPS (Zhang et al., 2018) between the input image and generated edit. Since fidelity to the input is ambiguous for editing tasks, where the output should preserve irrelevant content while changing the edited region, we also report FID on DragBench to measure overall visual quality and realism. For DragBench++, we instead report IF* against the reference edits as the primary fidelity metric.

sections.title: 4.2 COMPARISON WITH BASELINES
sections.content: Quantitative Evaluation. We compare against state-of-the-art drag-based image editing methods with public official implementations: test-time optimization methods DragDiffusion (Shi et al., 2024), DragNoise (Liu et al., 2024a), and DragLoRA (Xia et al., 2025); one-step methods FastDrag (Zhao et al., 2024) and GeoDrag (Pu et al., 2026); and fine-tuned conditional generation methods InstantDrag (Shin et al., 2024) and LightningDrag (Shi et al., 2025). Table 1 reports quantitative results on DragBench and DragBench++, with THINKDRAG in direct mode. Across both benchmarks, THINKDRAG achieves the best generation quality, with the highest IF and lowest FID on DragBench, and the best IF and IF* on DragBench++. On DragBench, THINKDRAG remains competitive in point-following accuracy, although the strongest MD scores come from test-time optimization and one-step methods that explicitly enforce the point displacement at inference. The advantage is clearer on DragBench++, where edits require stronger semantic interpretation. THINKDRAG achieves the best MD and MDMLLM. The reference row also shows that DIFT-based MD is less reliable in this setting, since even reference edits obtain relatively high MD. MDMLLM provides more semantic estimate, under which THINKDRAG substantially outperforms the baselines. The improvement in IF* further shows that THINKDRAG does not improve point accuracy by producing implausible distortions; its outputs remain closest to the reference edits. Qualitative Analysis. Figure 5 shows qualitative comparisons on DragBench and DragBench++. On DragBench, most methods handle relatively direct point movements, while THINKDRAG better preserves identity and local appearance during the edit. On DragBench++, the gap is more pronounced. Figure 6 compares direct generation with the reasoning mode. Direct generation already benefits from semantic drag supervision, but reasoning can provide an additional advantage when the transformation is under-specified by the points alone. In such cases, explicitly interpreting the edit before generation helps resolve ambiguity and coordinate non-local changes, such as opening refrigerator door or making waves taller in painting. User Study. We conduct user study with 30 participants, each answering 20 questions sampled evenly from DragBench and DragBench++. For each question, participants see the input image, the drag instruction, and anonymized outputs of DragLoRA, GeoDrag, LightningDrag, and THINKDRAG in random order, and select the preferred result for edit accuracy, generation quality, and overall preference. As shown in Table 3, participants clearly prefer THINKDRAG, with 80% of the overall-preference votes on DragBench++ and 61% on DragBench, an external benchmark independent of our data pipeline, and similar shares for the other criteria (Appendix B.3). On DragBench, THINKDRAG also receives 62% of the edit-accuracy votes despite higher DIFT-based MD than all three baselines, suggesting that MD does not fully capture semantic correctness. 4.3 JOINT TEXT-DRAG CONDITIONING In the default setting, THINKDRAG infers the intended edit from the input image and drag points alone, either directly or through its reasoning chain. Joint text-drag conditioning provides complementary mode where the user specifies part of the semantic intent. This is useful when the same point motion admits multiple plausible interpretations, since drag points provide spatial anchors while text clarifies the desired transformation. Prior work has explicitly targeted this setting with specialized mechanisms (Jiang et al., 2025). In THINKDRAG, it follows naturally from the unified multimodal formulation. During training, we condition the model on both drag endpoints and the corresponding text edit description for 10% of samples, allowing it to learn text-drag interaction without making text mandatory at inference time. As shown in Figure 7, the same drag instruction can be resolved into different valid edits when paired with different text prompts, such as widening flower versus opening its petals, or enlarging the candle body versus extending the flame.

Table 5 separates the contributions of the base model, the data, and DEM. Neither BAGEL nor the editing model FLUX.2 follows drag instructions zero-shot, and FLUX.2 attains high IF largely because it leaves the image unchanged. Training on our dataset without DEM substantially reduces MD, and adding DEM reduces it much further with similar IF and FID. This gap indicates that the structured text representation alone is insufficient for precise spatial control at this scale, and that endpoint markers provide important grounding. Training with textual drag coordinates nevertheless yields an emergent ability to ground coordinates in image content (Appendix A.3). Figure 8 further shows that without DEM the model still captures the overall intent of the drag instruction but lacks the spatial precision needed to align the edited content with the target point. The attention maps provide insight into this. Without DEM, the attention of the target location rarely peaks at the handle, resulting in the reduced precision observed. With DEM, the attention peaks at the handle for 51% of drags on DragBench++, compared to 6% without (Appendix A.4).

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced THINKDRAG, unified multimodal framework for drag-based image editing with visual reasoning. By training on new dataset of high-quality semantic drag transformations and reasoning traces, and by grounding each drag with Drag Endpoint Markers, THINKDRAG learns to interpret sparse point constraints in relation to scene content and object structure, rather than treating them only as geometric displacements. We also introduced DragBench++, benchmark of more challenging drag-based editing scenarios with reference edits. Experiments show that THINKDRAG achieves state-of-the-art generation quality while maintaining competitive point-following precision, with the reasoning mode providing additional interpretability, particularly for ambiguous multi-drag edits.

sections.content: A.1 ADDITIONAL VISUAL RESULTS Figure 9 provides additional qualitative comparisons on DragBench and DragBench++. For easier inspection of editing accuracy, we overlay the target points on the generated images. These examples further illustrate the ability of THINKDRAG to produce spatially accurate edits while preserving image identity and visual quality. A.2 REASONING ANALYSIS Table 6 reports the win rate of reasoning over direct generation on DragBench++, where mode wins sample if its output has the lower MDMLLM. Overall, the two modes win about equally often (reasoning wins 75 of the 145 samples, 51.7%), but reasoning wins on 56% of multi-drag edits compared with 36% of single-drag edits. Table 7 shows win rates across edit types. To assess faithfulness, Qwen3.6-27B judges whether each generated trace describes the same edit as the annotated edit prompt, and as control we construct deliberately incorrect edit prompt for each sample. The traces are judged consistent with the annotated prompt for 78.6% of samples and with the incorrect prompt for 2.8%. Since an ambiguous drag can admit several valid interpretations, the first number is conservative estimate of trace correctness. sections.title: B ADDITIONAL EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS
sections.content: B.

sections.title: IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: We implement THINKDRAG using BAGEL (Deng et al., 2025) as the base unified multimodal model. We train LoRA adapters (Hu et al., 2022) of rank 256 on the attention and MLP projections of the base transformer for 100K steps, using AdamW with learning rate of 2 105 and cosine schedule. The effective batch size is approximately 16 samples, distributed across 4 NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The training procedure takes around 60 hours. We set the reasoning loss weight to λthink = 0.25. We support up to 10 drag pairs per image during training; this limit is configurable. Unless otherwise specified, inference uses 50 sampling steps with classifier-free guidance scales of 3.0 for text and 1.5 for image conditioning. The learned endpoint scales remain close to their initialization (αtgt 1.16, αsrc 1.12). Images are processed at their native aspect ratio, with training images mostly square and the remainder in 4:3 and 16:9 in both orientations. The number of drags per sample (17) follows the annotation without random subsampling. The arrows and points drawn in our figures serve only as visualization, since the model receives drags solely as text and DEM. For the zero-shot rows of Table 5, BAGEL and FLUX.2 receive the drags as structured text instructions. B.2 MLLM-BASED EVALUATION For the MDMLLM metric, we use GPT-5.5 (OpenAI, 2026) to track source handle points in the generated image. The model receives the source image, the generated image, and the source handlepoint coordinates. It is prompted to return the corresponding physical or semantic point locations in the generated image using normalized coordinates in [0, 1000]. Due to API cost, we compute MDMLLM for the strongest method of each category (DragLoRA, GeoDrag, and LightningDrag), the same baselines as in the user study, and mark the remaining methods with in Table 1. Figure 11 compares this protocol with DIFT-based tracking. Although MLLM-based tracking is also imperfect, it is more robust in challenging cases involving semantic ambiguity, large structural changes, or visually similar distractors, where local feature matching can select an incorrect correspondence. On the reference edits of DragBench++, which satisfy their drags by construction, DIFT reports mean distance of 43.42, whereas GPT-5.5 reports 27.38. Most of the DIFT distance on this benchmark therefore reflects tracking failures under large structural changes. On DragBench, where edits are more local, DIFT remains accurate, so we report both trackers and regard them as complementary. Prompt for MLLM-based point tracking You are highly precise vision-language model. You see two images in order: SOURCE then GENERATED. Your task is point tracking. The user provides handle point coordinates in the SOURCE image. For each provided source handle point, return the corresponding same physical/semantic point location in the GENERATED image. Critical rules: - Track the exact same point or landmark. - The source handle point may have moved, deformed, or changed appearance in the generated image. - Use nearby object geometry, part boundaries, corners/tips/joints/hinges, texture, and semantic context to identify the correspondence. - If point is occluded or not visible in the GENERATED image, set its target to the nearest visible point. - Coordinates are normalized to 0-1000: (0,0) top-left, (1000,1000) bottom-right of the GENERATED image. - Return exactly one entry per input point, preserving the input point index. - Do not include markdown or prose. Output STRICT JSON: {"tracked_points":[{"index":0,"target":[x,y]}]}

B.3 USER STUDY Each of the 30 participants answered 20 questions sampled evenly from DragBench and DragBench++. For each question, edited results from different methods were anonymized and shown in random order. Edit accuracy measures how well the output follows the drag instruction and moves the intended content toward the target location. Generation quality measures whether the edited image remains faithful to the input, preserving identity, appearance, and unrelated regions while avoiding artifacts. Overall preference considers both criteria. We compare against DragLoRA, GeoDrag, and LightningDrag, the strongest baseline of each category. Table 11 reports all three criteria for each benchmark and for both benchmarks combined. Over both benchmarks, THINKDRAG receives about 70% of the votes under each criterion and the most votes on 18 of the 20 questions. Table 11: User study vote share (%) by benchmark and criterion. sections.title: User study instructions
sections.content: User Study on Drag-based Image Editing You will be shown 20 questions with an input image, drag instruction, and edited results. For each example, answer the following three questions: Editing Accuracy: Select the result that best follows the drag instruction. Focus on whether image content moves from the handle point to the target point and the intended edit is achieved. Generation Quality: Select the result with the best visual quality for the given edit. Focus on image quality, realism, lack of artifacts, and preservation of regions that should not change. Overall Preference: Select the result you prefer overall, considering both editing accuracy and generation quality. The edited results are shown in random order.

sections.title: D LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK
sections.content: While THINKDRAG achieves strong drag-based editing performance across both standard and challenging scenarios, several limitations remain. First, the reasoning mode introduces additional inference latency due to autoregressive reasoning generation, and its benefit is concentrated in ambiguous multi-drag edits. Although direct editing remains available and already performs strongly, future work could study distillation or adaptive reasoning strategies that invoke reasoning only when the edit is ambiguous. Second, our reasoning is expressed in language space, which provides interpretability but may not fully capture fine-grained visual transformations. promising direction is to explore reasoning directly in latent or pixel space, where intermediate representations could encode spatial transformations more explicitly. Finally, although DragBench++ expands evaluation toward more semantic and ambiguous edits, drag-based editing remains under-constrained, and automatic metrics only partially reflect human preference. Future benchmarks could develop more robust evaluation protocols for settings where multiple valid edits can satisfy the same instruction.
